On Lanai, one man's company holds 98 percent of the land, and in spring 2026 it asked the state to rezone about 170 acres at Koele, adding resort villas and spa units, an event space on ranch pasture, and an 83-acre public park on an old golf course. Some residents see a win: the resorts bring in money and good jobs for the people who live here. Others see a loss: Koele has long been the heart of the Hawaiian community on Lanai, and two old plantation homes near the resort have already been moved once before. When one landowner shapes nearly every plan on an island, should new jobs and a public park come first, or should the island's old places be left as they are? Which side do you lean toward, and why? Tell us where you are watching from today. 👇

comments.author: @u4tubular
comments.text: Before becoming a “wellness resort” for the rich, it was The Lodge at Koele which was a bit more affordable and was like staying at an English country estate complete with daily high tea. As small as the island is the shuttle ride down to the Manele Bay Hotel was rather long. When pineapple was king on the island it was the same situation of having the company control everything.

replies.author: @u4tubular
replies.text: @islandwanderer808Same here because my grandma moved there from Maui. Fond memories of snacking on venison jerky all day, arduous journeys by WWII era Jeeps to go camping, searching for tako, and night fishing at the harbor. As an adult I really did enjoy the venison carpaccio appetizer on the Lodge’s dinner menu, the fancy miniature golf, and stuffing myself at high tea haha! I never did get into hunting or serious golfing there like some of my friends. My hunting friends would stay at the Hotel Lanai sine they weren’t “honeymooning”.
